narrative: The model estimates a 92% chance that you will leave your job, which is why the promotion was denied: the decision treats you as a high retention risk rather than a certain leaver. The strongest signal was your overall work experience of 6–10 years. Compared with employees predicted to stay—where 1–5 years was the most common band—your longer overall experience pushed the prediction toward leaving. The second strongest signal was that you reported other job opportunities. This is uncommon among predicted stayers, only about one in four, so it sharply increased the leaving risk. Third, your 1–5 years in your current organization also contributed toward leaving, even though that tenure length is common among stayers; in your combination of circumstances, it added to the risk rather than offsetting it. All three top factors pointed in the same direction: toward leaving. Rather than treating this as a final judgment, the organization should review retention factors with you—career path, promotion fairness, recognition, pay satisfaction, and job stability—before deciding. You should also clarify whether those outside opportunities are genuinely better and raise any concerns about growth or support. A human review should confirm the promotion decision.
